Polynomials Hugging the Curve

This scene lays a polynomial over a curve. Raise the degree and it hugs the curve.

Match the value, the slope, and the bending at one point. The more you match, the better the imitation nearby. Far away, the imitation eventually breaks.

For example, knowing where a 🚗 car is, how fast it goes, and how it accelerates lets you predict its position a little later. More information predicts farther ahead.

Explain why Rn(x)→0R_n(x) \to 0Rn​(x)→0 is the heart of Taylor convergence. (Idea level)

f(x)=Tn(x)+Rn(x)f(x) = T_n(x) + R_n(x)f(x)=Tn​(x)+Rn​(x)
Show hint

  1. Taylor's theorem splits f(x)=Tn(x)+Rn(x)f(x) = T_n(x) + R_n(x)f(x)=Tn​(x)+Rn​(x). The polynomial part is what we know; the remainder is everything we don't.

  2. Exactly when Rn(x)→0R_n(x) \to 0Rn​(x)→0 do we get Tn(x)→f(x)T_n(x) \to f(x)Tn​(x)→f(x). The vanishing of the remainder IS the convergence of the series.

  3. Functions like sin⁡x\sin xsinx, whose remainder vanishes, match their Taylor series globally — but smooth functions exist where it doesn't. Mentioned at the idea level only.
